title: The Chemistry of Life and the Cell
bigQuestion: How can a bag of chemicals a few thousandths of a millimeter wide be alive?

story.title: The Cube That Could Not Get Bigger
story.kicker: Three jelly cubes go into the same dish of vinegar. Only one of them changes color all the way through. Why?
paragraphs: Ms. Delgado sets three cubes of pink gelatin on the lab bench. One cube is 1 centimeter on a side, one is 2 centimeters, and one is 3 centimeters. The pink color comes from an indicator dye mixed into the gelatin. The dye turns clear when acid reaches it. She drops all three cubes into one dish of vinegar and starts the timer.

After ten minutes she lifts the cubes out and slices each one in half. The smallest cube is clear all the way to the center. The middle cube is clear around the edge, with a pink core about the size of a pea. The largest cube has a wide pink center. The acid reached only a thin outer shell. The vinegar was the same. The time was the same. The size was not.

The students measure. Acid moved in about 5 millimeters in ten minutes, in every cube. For the small cube, 5 millimeters is the whole cube. For the big cube, 5 millimeters barely scratches the surface. A cube gets more surface as it grows, but it gets much more volume. Doubling the side makes four times the surface and eight times the inside.

A cell has the same problem. Food, oxygen and water come in through its surface. Wastes leave through its surface. Everything inside, the whole volume, needs to be fed. If a cell grew too big, its center would starve while its edges did fine. That is one reason cells stay small, and it is why a large animal is built from trillions of tiny cells instead of a few giant ones.

A living cell is a chemical factory that stays small so the loading docks can keep up with the floor. In this chapter you will look at what the factory is made of, how it is organized, how things get through its walls, and how it keeps its inside steady while the outside changes.
story.think: If a cell needed to be much larger, what shape could it take so that no part of the inside was far from the surface?

lessons.title: Water Is Not Just Wet
lessons.mainIdea: Water's lopsided charge lets it stick to itself and dissolve almost everything a cell needs.
reading: Drop a paper clip flat onto still water and it floats. Steel is far denser than water, so it should sink. It floats because the surface of water acts like a thin, stretchy skin. That skin exists because water molecules pull on each other. A water molecule is one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, bent like a boomerang. The oxygen end carries a small negative charge and the hydrogen ends carry a small positive charge. A molecule with charged ends like this is called *polar*.

Opposite charges attract, so the hydrogen of one water molecule is pulled toward the oxygen of the next. This weak pull is a *hydrogen bond*. Each bond is easy to break, but there are so many that together they make water cling to itself. Scientists call that clinging *cohesion*. Cohesion holds the paper clip up, pulls water up a paper towel, and lets a column of water climb from a tree's roots to its leaves without breaking.

The same charges make water a powerful *solvent*, a liquid that dissolves other things. Salt, sugar, oxygen gas and thousands of the molecules a cell uses are polar or charged, so water molecules surround them and pull them apart. Roughly 60 percent of an adult human body is water. Almost every reaction in a cell happens with the ingredients dissolved in it. Oils are not polar, so water will not mix with them. That refusal, as you will see, is exactly what a cell membrane is built on.

Hydrogen bonds also make water slow to heat and slow to cool. A lake takes weeks to warm in spring, which is why Chicago's lakefront stays cooler than the suburbs in June. Your body, mostly water, resists sudden temperature swings the same way. And when water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open pattern that takes up more space, so ice floats. A pond freezes from the top down and the fish below stay in liquid water all winter.

words.d: having a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, like a water molecule
a weak attraction between the positive end of one molecule and the negative end of another
the tendency of water molecules to stick to one another
a liquid that dissolves other substances

look.title: The Tree That Lifts Water
look.text: A tall oak in an Illinois forest moves many liters of water from its roots to its leaves every summer day. There is no pump in the trunk. Water evaporates from the leaves, and the water column below is pulled up behind it, molecule after molecule, through tubes thinner than a hair.
look.prompt: Which property of water lets a column of it be pulled up a tree without snapping? What would happen if water molecules did not attract each other?

check.q: Why does a paper clip float on water even though steel is denser than water?
choices: Water molecules attract each other and form a skin-like surface
The paper clip is hollow and full of air
Water pushes up on steel more than on other metals
The paper clip is lighter than the water it displaces
check.why: Cohesion between water molecules creates surface tension that holds up the light clip. Steel itself does sink if it breaks through the surface.

check.q: Salt dissolves in water but oil does not. What best explains the difference?
choices: Oil is heavier than salt
Salt is made of charged particles that polar water molecules can pull apart; oil is not polar
Water is too cold to dissolve oil
Salt is a liquid and oil is a solid
check.why: Water dissolves polar and charged substances. Oil molecules have no charged ends for water to grab.

check.q: A pond freezes in January. What happens to the water under the ice, and why does it matter?
choices: It freezes solid from the bottom up, so fish move to the surface
It boils from pressure, so fish must surface to breathe
It stays liquid because ice floats and insulates the water below, so fish survive
It drains into the ground, so the pond empties
check.why: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it forms on top. The layer of ice shields the liquid water below from the cold air.

lessons.title: Carbon Builds the Big Molecules
lessons.mainIdea: Carbon's four bonds let cells build long chains, and four families of these chains make up almost everything alive.
reading: Burn a marshmallow, a leaf, or a strip of bacon and each one turns black. The black is carbon. Every living thing is built mostly from carbon, and the reason is a simple counting fact. A carbon atom can form four bonds. It can link to four other atoms, or to other carbons in chains, branches and rings, and still have room to attach hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. No other common element builds such large, stable, varied molecules.

Cells assemble small carbon units into giant ones called *macromolecules*, the way a train is built from cars. *Carbohydrates* are chains of sugar units. Glucose, a single sugar ring, is the fuel most cells burn. Plants link thousands of glucose units into starch for storage and into cellulose for their tough walls. Your body stores glucose chains as glycogen in liver and muscle.

*Lipids* are the fats, oils and waxes. Most are long chains of carbon and hydrogen with almost no oxygen, so they are not polar and water will not dissolve them. That makes them good for storing energy in a compact form and for building membranes. A special lipid with one polar end and one oily end, the phospholipid, is the main material of every cell membrane you own.

The other two families, proteins and nucleic acids, do the cell's work and hold its instructions. They get their own lesson. For now, notice the pattern: a few kinds of small units, joined in different orders and lengths, make an almost endless variety of large molecules. Every organism on Earth uses the same four families. That shared chemistry is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that all life is related.

words.d: a very large molecule built from many smaller repeating units
a sugar or a chain of sugars, such as glucose, starch or cellulose
a fat, oil or wax; a nonpolar molecule that does not dissolve in water
a single sugar molecule that most cells use as fuel

look.title: What a Human Body Is Made Of
look.prompt: Oxygen is the biggest number. Most of that oxygen is in water. Why do scientists still call life carbon-based rather than oxygen-based?

check.q: Why is carbon the backbone of the molecules of life?
choices: It is the most common element on Earth
It is the lightest element
It dissolves easily in water
Each carbon atom can form four bonds, allowing long stable chains and rings
check.why: Four bonds per atom let carbon build the large, varied structures that cells need. Carbon is common in life, not the most common element on Earth.

check.q: Starch, cellulose and glycogen are all made from the same small unit. What is it?
choices: Glucose
Amino acids
Fatty acids
Phosphate
check.why: All three are chains of glucose, joined in different ways for storage or structure.

check.q: A student says fats are useless because they do not dissolve in water. What is wrong with that claim?
choices: Fats do dissolve in water if you stir hard enough
Not dissolving in water is exactly what makes lipids good for energy storage and for building membranes
Fats are actually carbohydrates
Cells never contain any lipids
check.why: Lipids' refusal to mix with water lets them form membranes that separate the cell from its surroundings and store energy compactly.

lessons.title: Proteins and the Code That Makes Them
lessons.mainIdea: Proteins do the cell's work, and the order of their amino acids is written in DNA.
reading: Crack an egg into a hot pan and the clear liquid turns white and firm. Nothing was added. Heat changed the shape of the egg's proteins, and shape is everything for a protein. A *protein* is a chain of small units called *amino acids*. There are 20 kinds of amino acids, and a typical protein links a few hundred of them in a specific order. The chain then folds into a precise three-dimensional shape, and that shape decides what the protein can do.

Proteins are the cell's tools and machines. Some are structural, like the collagen in your skin and the keratin in your hair. Some carry things: hemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen. Some are gates in membranes. Some receive signals, and some, the enzymes, run chemical reactions. A single human cell contains thousands of different proteins, each with a job set by its folded shape. Heat, acid or the wrong salt level can unfold a protein, which is why a high fever is dangerous.

Where does a cell get the recipe for each protein? From its *nucleic acids*, the fourth family of macromolecules. *DNA* is a long double chain built from four kinds of units, called bases and lettered A, T, G and C. The order of those letters spells out the order of amino acids in every protein. A working copy of a gene is made in a related molecule, RNA, which carries the recipe out to the cell's protein-building machines.

One cell of yours holds about 2 meters of DNA. It is coiled and packed into a nucleus far smaller than the dot on this i. Every cell in your body carries the same DNA. But a skin cell and a nerve cell read different pages of it. That is the idea to keep. Proteins do the work. DNA stores the instructions. The same set of instructions can be read in different ways.

words.d: a folded chain of amino acids that does a specific job in the cell
one of 20 small building-block molecules that link to form proteins
DNA or RNA; a long molecule that stores or carries genetic instructions
the double-stranded molecule that holds the instructions for building proteins

look.title: Twenty Letters, Endless Words
look.text: Imagine an alphabet with 20 letters and no limit on word length. A word of just 5 letters can be spelled 3,200,000 different ways. Real proteins run to hundreds of letters. Now imagine that each spelling folds into its own shape, and only the right shape works.
look.prompt: Why might changing just one amino acid in a protein sometimes cause no harm, and other times stop the protein from working at all?

check.q: What decides what a protein can do?
choices: Its color
How much water it contains
The three-dimensional shape it folds into
The number of carbon atoms in it
check.why: A protein's folded shape lets it grip a particular molecule, form a particular structure or open a particular gate.

check.q: Why does a cooked egg white turn from clear to solid white?
choices: Water is boiled out of it
The egg white turns into fat
Sugar in the egg caramelizes
Heat unfolds the proteins, which tangle together into a solid mass
check.why: Heat breaks the weak bonds that hold each protein in shape. The unfolded chains stick to each other.

check.q: A skin cell and a nerve cell in the same person have the same DNA. How can they be so different?
choices: They read different genes from the same DNA and so make different proteins
Nerve cells have twice as much DNA
Skin cells lose most of their DNA as they age
Nerve cells contain RNA but no DNA
check.why: All body cells share the same instructions. Which genes are switched on determines which proteins get made.

lessons.title: Enzymes Make It Fast
lessons.mainIdea: Enzymes are proteins that speed up specific reactions by lowering the energy needed to start them.
reading: Put a drop of hydrogen peroxide on a cut and it foams. Put the same drop on the counter and nothing happens for hours. Your blood and skin cells contain an *enzyme* called catalase. It grabs hydrogen peroxide molecules and splits them into water and oxygen gas thousands of times per second. The foam is the oxygen. Hydrogen peroxide would break down on its own eventually, but far too slowly to matter. The enzyme does not change what happens. It changes how fast.

Almost every reaction in a cell needs a push to get started, an energy hill called *activation energy*. An enzyme lowers that hill. It has a pocket, the *active site*, shaped to fit one particular molecule, its *substrate*. When the substrate settles into the active site, the enzyme bends it or holds it next to a partner, and the reaction happens with much less push. The product leaves, and the enzyme, unchanged, grabs the next substrate.

Because the fit is so exact, each enzyme usually handles one job. Amylase in your saliva breaks starch into sugars, which is why a cracker tastes sweet after you chew it for a while. Lactase breaks down milk sugar, and people who stop making it become lactose intolerant. Pepsin works only in the strong acid of the stomach. Move an enzyme out of its normal temperature or acidity and its shape shifts, the active site no longer fits, and the reaction slows or stops.

For a long time nobody knew what enzymes were made of. In 1926 the American chemist James Sumner ground up jack beans, purified the enzyme urease, and coaxed it into crystals. The crystals were pure protein. That settled the question, and Sumner later shared a Nobel Prize for it. Today enzymes are used to make cheese, soften jeans, brew beer, remove stains in cold water and copy DNA in every genetics lab on Earth.

words.d: a protein that speeds up a specific chemical reaction without being used up
the energy needed to get a chemical reaction started
the pocket on an enzyme where its substrate fits
the molecule an enzyme acts on

look.title: An Enzyme in Crystal Form
look.text: Sumner reported that the crystals he had grown from jack bean extract dissolved to give a solution with powerful urease activity, and that every test showed the crystals to be protein. He concluded that the enzyme itself was a protein, something many chemists had doubted.
look.cite: James B. Sumner, paper on the isolation and crystallization of urease, Journal of Biological Chemistry, 1926
look.prompt: Why was getting a pure crystal such strong evidence? What could Sumner test on a crystal that he could not test on a messy bean extract?

check.q: What does an enzyme actually change about a chemical reaction?
choices: It changes the products that form
It lowers the activation energy so the reaction happens much faster
It adds energy to the cell
It makes the reaction happen only once
check.why: Enzymes do not change what reaction happens or its final products. They lower the energy barrier so it happens quickly.

check.q: Why does a cracker begin to taste sweet after you chew it for a minute?
choices: Sugar from your saliva soaks into it
Chewing heats the starch and melts it
Amylase in saliva breaks the cracker's starch into sugars
The salt on the cracker dissolves away
check.why: Amylase is an enzyme in saliva whose substrate is starch. Its products are sugars you can taste.

check.q: Pepsin works in the stomach at a very low pH. If pepsin were moved into the small intestine, which is not acidic, what would most likely happen?
choices: It would work faster because there is more food
It would begin breaking down starch instead
It would turn into a different enzyme
Its shape would change and it would stop working well
check.why: An enzyme's active site depends on its folded shape, and that shape depends on conditions like pH.

lessons.title: Every Living Thing Is Made of Cells
lessons.mainIdea: Cell theory took two centuries of microscopes and argument: all living things are made of cells, and every cell comes from another cell.
reading: In 1665 the English scientist Robert Hooke sliced a thin sliver of cork, put it under a microscope he had built, and saw rows of tiny empty boxes. They reminded him of the small rooms, or cells, that monks lived in, so he called them cells. The name stuck. What Hooke saw were the dead walls of plant cells, but it was the first time anyone had described the box-like units that living things are built from.

A decade later a Dutch cloth merchant, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, ground lenses so fine that he could see single living creatures swimming in a drop of pond water. He called them animalcules, little animals. He found them in rain, in scrapings from his teeth, and in almost every liquid he looked at. Nobody had imagined a whole world too small to see. Many scientists did not believe him until they looked for themselves.

It took nearly two more centuries to turn these sightings into a rule. In 1838 the botanist Matthias Schleiden argued that all plants are made of cells. In 1839 Theodor Schwann showed the same for animals. In 1855 the physician Rudolf Virchow added the last piece: every cell comes from a cell that already existed. Cells do not form from slime or dust. They divide. Together these ideas are the *cell theory*: all living things are made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from other cells.

Cell theory sounds obvious now, but it changed medicine. If cells come only from cells, then disease is something that happens to cells. A tumor is cells dividing when they should not. An infection is foreign cells multiplying inside you. Virchow's line, all cells from cells, is still the foundation of pathology, the science of what goes wrong in the body.

words.d: the idea that all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from other cells
the smallest unit of a living thing that can carry out the processes of life
the study of what goes wrong in cells and tissues during disease

look.title: Hooke Looks at Cork
look.text: Hooke wrote that when he examined a thin slice of cork with his microscope, he could clearly see it was full of pores, like a honeycomb, though the holes were not regular. These pores, or cells, he said, were the first tiny pores he had ever seen, and perhaps the first anyone had seen, since no earlier writer had mentioned them.
look.prompt: Hooke saw only empty walls because cork is dead tissue. What did he miss, and why would it have been hard to guess from cork alone that these boxes were once alive?

check.q: Why did Robert Hooke choose the word cell for what he saw in cork?
choices: The tiny boxes reminded him of the small rooms monks lived in
He saw them dividing
He could see a nucleus inside each one
The word means small in Latin
check.why: Hooke saw empty compartments, which looked to him like the rows of small rooms in a monastery.

check.q: Which statement is part of cell theory?
choices: Only animals are made of cells
All cells come from cells that already existed
Cells can form on their own from nonliving matter
Every cell has a nucleus
check.why: Virchow's rule that cells come only from other cells is the third part of cell theory. Bacteria are cells with no nucleus.

check.q: How did cell theory change the way doctors think about disease?
choices: It showed that disease is caused by bad air
It proved that all diseases are inherited
It suggested that disease is something that happens to cells, such as cells dividing when they should not
It showed that sick cells are not really cells
check.why: If all cells come from cells, a tumor or infection is a story about cells multiplying, and that is where to look for causes and cures.

lessons.title: Two Kinds of Cells
lessons.mainIdea: Prokaryotic cells are small and have no nucleus; eukaryotic cells are larger and divide their work among membrane-wrapped compartments.
reading: Scrape the inside of your cheek onto a slide and stain it. Under the microscope you see wide, flat cells, each with a dark dot near the middle. Now look at a drop of yogurt. The living things there are hundreds of times smaller, plain rods and spheres with no dot at all. You have just seen the two great kinds of cells on Earth. The dot is a *nucleus*, a membrane-wrapped compartment holding the cell's DNA. Cells with a nucleus are *eukaryotic*. Cells without one are *prokaryotic*.

Prokaryotes are bacteria and their less familiar cousins, the archaea. A typical bacterium is 1 to 5 micrometers long; a micrometer is one thousandth of a millimeter. Its DNA is a single loop floating in the cytoplasm. It has a tough cell wall, a membrane, ribosomes to build proteins, and often a whip-like flagellum to swim with. That is nearly the whole list. Prokaryotes are simple, but they are not primitive failures. They have lived on Earth for more than 3 billion years, and there are more bacterial cells in your gut than human cells in your whole body.

Eukaryotic cells are usually 10 to 100 micrometers across, ten times wider than a bacterium and often a thousand times the volume. Animals, plants, fungi and protists are all eukaryotes. Besides the nucleus, their cytoplasm holds *organelles*, small structures wrapped in their own membranes, each doing a specialized job. Remember the surface-to-volume problem from the chapter story. Organelles are part of the answer. Folding membranes inside the cell adds enormous surface area where reactions can happen.

Two organelles, mitochondria and chloroplasts, have their own small loops of DNA and their own ribosomes, and they look strikingly like bacteria. Most biologists accept the explanation that they once were bacteria. Long ago, an early eukaryotic cell swallowed them and, instead of digesting them, kept them. This idea, endosymbiosis, was argued most forcefully by Lynn Margulis in the 1960s and was doubted for years before the DNA evidence made it convincing.

words.d: the membrane-wrapped compartment in a eukaryotic cell that holds the DNA
describing a cell with no nucleus and no membrane-wrapped organelles, such as a bacterium
describing a cell with a nucleus and organelles, as in animals, plants and fungi
a small structure inside a eukaryotic cell that does a specialized job

look.title: How Big Is a Cell?
look.prompt: About how many bacteria could line up end to end across one cheek cell? Which of these cells could you see with your unaided eye?

check.q: What is the single clearest difference between a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell?
choices: Prokaryotes are always harmful
Eukaryotes have no cell membrane
Prokaryotes cannot make proteins
Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and prokaryotic cells do not
check.why: The nucleus, a membrane-wrapped compartment for DNA, is the defining feature of eukaryotes.

check.q: Mitochondria have their own DNA and ribosomes and resemble bacteria. What do most biologists conclude from this?
choices: Mitochondria descended from bacteria that were taken inside an early eukaryotic cell
Mitochondria are infections that cells fight off
Bacteria are made of mitochondria
Mitochondria are not really part of the cell
check.why: The endosymbiosis explanation fits the DNA evidence, the double membranes and the bacterial-style ribosomes.

check.q: A eukaryotic cell may be a thousand times the volume of a bacterium. How do organelles help it cope with the surface-to-volume problem?
choices: They make the cell smaller
Their folded internal membranes add a great deal of surface area where reactions can happen
They pump water out of the cell
They replace the need for a cell membrane
check.why: Membranes inside the cell give it far more working surface than its outer membrane alone.

lessons.title: Division of Labor Inside a Cell
lessons.mainIdea: Each organelle does one kind of job, and the kind of cell decides which organelles it has the most of.
reading: Think of a eukaryotic cell as a small city. The nucleus is city hall, where the master plans, the DNA, are kept and copied. Orders leave the nucleus as RNA and go to the *ribosomes*, tiny factories that string amino acids into proteins. Some ribosomes float free. Many sit on a folded membrane maze called the endoplasmic reticulum, which finishes, folds and ships the proteins. A stack of flattened sacs, the Golgi apparatus, sorts and packages them for delivery inside or outside the cell.

*Mitochondria* are the power plants. They take in sugar and oxygen and release the energy in a form the cell can spend, a molecule called ATP. Cells that do a lot of work carry a lot of them. A heart muscle cell may be packed with thousands. Lysosomes are the recycling plants, small bags of enzymes that break down worn-out parts and swallowed bacteria. The *cytoskeleton*, a network of protein fibers, is the framework of roads and girders that holds the shape and moves things around.

Plant cells have three extras. A *chloroplast* is a green organelle that captures sunlight and builds sugar, the subject of the next chapter. A large central *vacuole* holds water and keeps the cell firm, which is why a well-watered plant stands up and a dry one droops. And outside the membrane sits a stiff cell wall of cellulose. Animal cells have none of these. Bacteria have a wall too, but of a different material, which is why some antibiotics can attack bacteria without harming your cells.

Look at a cell's organelles and you can guess its job. A cell in your pancreas that makes digestive enzymes is crowded with endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi. A sperm cell is little more than a nucleus, a tail and a ring of mitochondria to power it. A leaf cell in the sun is stuffed with chloroplasts, while a root cell of the same plant has none. Same organism, same DNA, different equipment for different work.

words.d: a tiny structure that builds proteins by linking amino acids in the order the RNA specifies
the organelle that releases energy from food and stores it as ATP (plural: mitochondria)
the green organelle in plant cells that captures light energy to make sugar
a large water-filled sac in plant cells that stores substances and keeps the cell firm
a network of protein fibers that gives a cell its shape and moves parts within it

look.title: Guess the Cell
look.text: Under a powerful microscope, three unknown cells are photographed. Cell A is long and thin, with mitochondria lined up in rows along its whole length. Cell B is round, has a huge central vacuole, a thick outer wall and green organelles. Cell C is small, has no nucleus, and has a single loop of DNA and a tail.
look.prompt: What kind of cell is each one most likely to be, and what job does its equipment suggest?

check.q: Which organelle builds proteins?
choices: The vacuole
The chloroplast
The ribosome
The lysosome
check.why: Ribosomes link amino acids into protein chains, following the order carried by RNA.

check.q: A heart muscle cell contains far more mitochondria than a skin cell. What is the best explanation?
choices: Heart cells are larger
Heart cells store more DNA
Heart cells make more proteins
Heart cells work constantly and need much more ATP
check.why: Mitochondria supply ATP. Cells that use energy nonstop are packed with them.

check.q: A houseplant droops when it has not been watered. Which organelle is most directly involved?
choices: The central vacuole, which loses water and no longer presses the cell firm
The nucleus, which stops copying DNA
The mitochondrion, which runs out of oxygen
The ribosome, which stops making proteins
check.why: A full vacuole pushes outward against the cell wall and keeps the plant upright. An emptying vacuole lets the cells go limp.

lessons.title: Making the Invisible Visible
lessons.mainIdea: A microscope magnifies, a stain adds contrast, and resolution, not magnification, sets what you can actually see.
reading: Hooke's microscope magnified a few dozen times. A classroom microscope today, like the one on this site, uses a 10x eyepiece and a set of objective lenses. Multiply the two numbers to get the total. A 4x objective gives 40x, enough to see a whole insect wing. The 40x objective gives 400x, where cheek cells fill the view and their nuclei show clearly. The 100x objective, used with a drop of oil between lens and slide, gives 1,000x, about the limit for a light microscope.

Magnifying more does not always show more. Every microscope has a *resolution* limit, the smallest gap between two points that it can still show as two points instead of one blur. For light microscopes that limit is about 0.2 micrometers, set by the wavelength of visible light itself. Blow the image up past that and it just gets bigger and fuzzier. To see the ribosomes, the membranes, or a virus, you need an electron microscope, which uses a beam of electrons with a much shorter wavelength and can resolve details thousands of times finer.

The other problem is that most cells are nearly transparent. Water in water is hard to see. So microscopists use *stains*, dyes that stick to particular parts. Methylene blue binds to DNA and turns the nucleus a deep blue. Iodine turns starch grains in a potato cell almost black. In 1884 the Danish doctor Hans Christian Gram found a stain that turns some bacteria purple and others pink, depending on the chemistry of their cell walls. Gram staining is still one of the first tests a hospital lab runs on a sample.

Staining usually kills the cell, so a stained slide is a snapshot, not a movie. Modern labs get around that by attaching glowing fluorescent tags to specific proteins in living cells and filming them. But the logic has not changed since Hooke. Magnify enough to see the structure, add contrast so it stands out, and be honest about what the instrument can and cannot resolve.

words.d: how many times larger an image appears than the object; eyepiece power times objective power
the smallest distance between two points that a microscope can still show as separate
a dye that binds to part of a cell so that it stands out from the rest
the lens on a microscope nearest the specimen

look.title: Total Magnification on a Classroom Microscope
look.prompt: A red blood cell is about 8 micrometers wide. At 400x, how wide would it appear? Why would going to 4,000x not let you see the cell's ribosomes?

check.q: A microscope has a 10x eyepiece and you choose the 40x objective. What is the total magnification?
check.why: Total magnification is eyepiece power times objective power: 10 times 40 equals 400.

check.q: Why can a light microscope not show a virus clearly, no matter how strong the lenses are?
choices: Viruses are transparent
Viruses move too fast
Visible light's wavelength limits resolution to about 0.2 micrometers, and viruses are smaller than that
Viruses are only visible in color
check.why: Resolution, not magnification, is the limit. Electron microscopes use shorter wavelengths to resolve finer detail.

check.q: Why do biologists add a stain like methylene blue to cheek cells before looking at them?
choices: To keep the cells alive longer
To make the cells larger
To kill any bacteria on the slide
To add contrast so the nucleus and other parts stand out from the clear cytoplasm
check.why: Most cell contents are nearly transparent. A stain binds to certain parts and makes them visible.

lessons.title: The Gatekeeper Membrane
lessons.mainIdea: The cell membrane is a two-layer sheet of phospholipids studded with proteins, and it lets some things through and not others.
reading: Shake oil and water in a jar and they separate again in seconds. That separation is the cell's oldest trick. A *phospholipid* is a molecule with a polar head that loves water and two long oily tails that avoid it. Put millions of them in water and they arrange themselves so that every tail is hidden from water and every head touches it. The result is a double layer, the *bilayer*, with tails sandwiched in the middle. It forms on its own, and it heals its own tears.

That bilayer is the *cell membrane*. It is about 7 to 8 nanometers thick, so thin that a stack of ten thousand would be about the thickness of a sheet of paper. Because the middle of the sheet is oily, water-loving things like sugar, salt ions and proteins cannot pass through it on their own. Small nonpolar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide slip through easily. That is what scientists mean when they call the membrane *selectively permeable*: some things get through, some do not.

The membrane is not a plain sheet. Proteins are embedded in it like boats in a harbor, and they can drift sideways, which is why the standard picture is called the fluid mosaic model. Some proteins are channels, tunnels lined with polar groups so that ions or water can pass. Some are carriers that grab a molecule on one side and release it on the other. Some are receptors that catch a signal outside and pass the message inside. Some are identity tags that tell your immune system this cell belongs to you.

Every cell has a membrane. Eukaryotic cells have many more inside, around the nucleus and each organelle. All of them use the same bilayer design. Understanding that one thin, oily, self-sealing sheet explains a lot. It explains why sugar you drink takes time to reach your blood. It explains why anesthetic gases, which are nonpolar, slip into nerve cells so easily. And it explains how a cell keeps an inside chemistry completely different from the outside.

words.d: a lipid with a water-loving head and two water-avoiding tails; the main building block of membranes
a double layer of phospholipids with the oily tails in the middle
the thin phospholipid-and-protein boundary that surrounds every cell
letting some substances pass through while blocking others

look.title: A Sheet That Builds Itself
look.text: In a lab, pure phospholipids are dropped into water and gently shaken. Within moments they form hollow spheres, each bounded by a bilayer, with water inside and water outside. Nobody assembled them. Scientists can load these spheres with medicine and inject them; some vaccines and cancer drugs are delivered this way.
look.prompt: Why do the phospholipids arrange themselves into a double layer rather than a single layer or a random tangle? What does this suggest about how the first cells might have gotten their boundaries?

check.q: Why do phospholipids in water form a double layer with the tails inside?
choices: The polar heads stay in contact with water while the oily tails avoid it
The tails are heavier and sink to the middle
Proteins push the tails together
The heads are attracted to each other by magnetism
check.why: Water-avoiding tails hide from water and water-loving heads face it. The bilayer is the arrangement that satisfies both.

check.q: Oxygen crosses a membrane easily but a sugar molecule cannot cross on its own. Why?
choices: Oxygen is a solid
Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it passes through the oily middle; sugar is polar and is blocked
Sugar is too heavy to move
Oxygen is pulled in by the nucleus
check.why: The oily core of the bilayer admits small nonpolar molecules and repels polar or charged ones, which need protein help.

check.q: What does the phrase fluid mosaic mean when describing a cell membrane?
choices: The membrane is made of liquid water
The membrane is a rigid grid of tiles
The membrane is a flexible sheet of lipids with proteins scattered through it that can drift sideways
The membrane dissolves and re-forms every second
check.why: Fluid refers to the lipids' ability to flow; mosaic refers to the mix of proteins embedded among them.

lessons.title: Diffusion and Osmosis
lessons.mainIdea: Molecules spread from where they are crowded to where they are not, and when water does this across a membrane, cells swell or shrink.
reading: Someone opens a bottle of perfume at the front of the room. Thirty seconds later the back row smells it. No fan moved the air. Molecules are always jiggling, and random jiggling spreads them out from where they are crowded to where they are scarce. This is *diffusion*. It happens on its own, with no energy spent by anyone, and it stops only when the molecules are evenly spread. The difference in crowding between two places is called a *concentration gradient*, and diffusion always runs down the gradient.

Diffusion is how oxygen gets into your blood and carbon dioxide gets out. Air in the lungs has more oxygen than blood does, so oxygen diffuses across the thin lung lining into the blood. Blood arriving at a muscle has more oxygen than the working muscle, so it diffuses out again. Ions and sugars, which cannot slip through the oily membrane, diffuse through channel and carrier proteins instead. That is called facilitated diffusion, but it still runs downhill and costs the cell nothing.

Water diffuses too, and water crossing a membrane gets its own name: *osmosis*. Water moves toward the side where dissolved particles are more concentrated, because that is where the water itself is less concentrated. Sprinkle salt on a slice of cucumber and it weeps. The salt outside draws water out of the cells. Drop a wilted lettuce leaf into plain water and it stiffens, because water flows into its cells until each vacuole presses hard against the cell wall. Plant cells depend on that pressure to stand up.

Animal cells have no wall, so osmosis can be dangerous. A red blood cell dropped into pure water swells until it bursts. Dropped into strong salt water, it shrivels. That is why hospitals give fluids in a solution with the same total concentration as blood, called *isotonic*, about 0.9 percent salt. It is also why drinking seawater makes you thirstier: the salt pulls water out of your cells and your kidneys need extra water to flush it out.

words.d: the spreading of molecules from an area of higher concentration to lower concentration
a difference in concentration between two places
the diffusion of water across a membrane toward the side with more dissolved particles
having the same concentration of dissolved particles as the inside of a cell

look.title: The Slug and the Salt
look.text: A slug on a wet Illinois sidewalk is mostly water held inside thin-skinned cells. A child sprinkles table salt on it. Within seconds the slug shrinks and a puddle of fluid appears around it. The salt did not burn anything or poison anything.
look.prompt: Explain what happened to the slug's cells in terms of osmosis. Which way did water move, and why?

check.q: Which of the following is diffusion?
choices: A pump moving sugar into a cell using ATP
A plant pulling water up its stem
The nucleus sending RNA to a ribosome
Oxygen spreading from air in the lungs into blood that has less oxygen
check.why: Diffusion is the passive spread of molecules down a concentration gradient. Oxygen entering the blood is a classic example.

check.q: A red blood cell is dropped into pure water. What happens and why?
choices: It swells and may burst, because water moves in toward the higher concentration of dissolved particles inside
It shrivels, because water leaves the cell
Nothing, because red blood cells have cell walls
It divides, because water triggers mitosis
check.why: Inside the cell there are many dissolved particles; outside there are none. Water flows in by osmosis and the cell cannot resist.

check.q: Why does a wilted lettuce leaf become crisp again in a bowl of water?
choices: The leaf absorbs oxygen from the water
Water enters the cells by osmosis and the full vacuoles press against the cell walls
The cold water shrinks the cells
The leaf begins photosynthesis
check.why: Plant cells become firm when their vacuoles fill with water and push outward against the wall.

lessons.title: Moving Things Uphill
lessons.mainIdea: Cells spend energy to pump molecules against their gradients and to swallow or release whole packages.
reading: A nerve cell keeps far more potassium inside than outside, and far more sodium outside than inside. Diffusion is trying to erase both differences every second. The cell fights back with a protein pump. The sodium-potassium pump grabs three sodium ions from inside, uses one molecule of ATP, changes shape, and shoves them out. Then it takes two potassium ions from outside and brings them in. Moving molecules against their concentration gradient, using energy, is *active transport*.

Active transport is expensive. A resting nerve cell spends a large share of its ATP just running these pumps, which is part of why the brain, only about 2 percent of your body weight, burns roughly 20 percent of your energy at rest. But the gradients are worth it. The stored difference in charge across a nerve membrane is what lets a nerve fire. Kidney cells use active transport to pull salt back out of urine. Root cells use it to draw scarce minerals from soil into the plant.

Some cargo is far too big for any channel or pump. For that, the membrane itself moves. In *endocytosis*, the membrane folds inward around a particle, pinches off, and the particle floats inside the cell in a bubble of membrane called a vesicle. White blood cells eat bacteria this way, a form of endocytosis called phagocytosis. The reverse, *exocytosis*, lets a vesicle fuse with the membrane and dump its contents outside. That is how nerve cells release their signal chemicals and how pancreas cells release insulin.

Put the two lessons together and the membrane is a sorting system with several speeds. Small nonpolar molecules diffuse straight through. Ions and sugars diffuse through proteins, still for free. Things that need to go uphill get pumped, at a cost in ATP. Big packages are swallowed or spat out whole. The cell membrane is thinner than any material a person has ever manufactured, yet it does all of that at once.

words.d: moving substances across a membrane against their concentration gradient using energy from ATP
the molecule cells use to store and spend energy for work
the process in which a cell's membrane folds inward to swallow a particle
the process in which a vesicle fuses with the cell membrane to release its contents outside

look.title: A Pump That Never Stops
look.text: Picture a rowboat with a slow leak. The water outside is trying to get in, and it will, drop by drop, forever. The only way to keep the boat dry is to bail, and bailing takes muscle. Stop bailing for an hour and the boat fills. A nerve cell is that boat, sodium is the water, and the sodium-potassium pump is the person bailing.
look.prompt: What would happen to a nerve cell if it ran out of ATP? Why is a poison that stops ATP production so quickly fatal?

check.q: What makes active transport different from diffusion?
choices: Active transport moves only water
Active transport only happens in plant cells
Active transport moves substances against their gradient and uses energy
Active transport does not need proteins
check.why: Diffusion runs downhill for free. Active transport runs uphill, powered by ATP through pump proteins.

check.q: A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium. Which process is this?
choices: Osmosis
Exocytosis
Facilitated diffusion
Endocytosis (phagocytosis)
check.why: The membrane folds around the bacterium and pinches off inside the cell, which is endocytosis.

check.q: The brain is about 2 percent of body weight but uses about 20 percent of the body's resting energy. What explains a large part of this?
choices: Nerve cells constantly run pumps to keep sodium and potassium gradients across their membranes
Nerve cells are much larger than other cells
The brain stores most of the body's fat
Nerve cells have no mitochondria and must borrow energy
check.why: Maintaining ion gradients by active transport costs ATP every second, and the brain has enormous numbers of nerve cells doing it.

lessons.title: A Steady Inside in a Changing World
lessons.mainIdea: Homeostasis is the constant work of keeping conditions inside the body within narrow limits while the outside changes.
reading: Step out of a warm building onto a Chicago sidewalk in January with a wind off the lake. The air might be minus 20 degrees Celsius. Your core stays close to 37 degrees. Step into a July heat wave and your core is still close to 37. The outside swings by more than 50 degrees; the inside barely moves. Keeping the inside steady while the outside changes is *homeostasis*, and every living thing does it, from a bacterium to an oak.

The French physiologist Claude Bernard noticed this in the 1860s. He argued that complex animals live in two environments at once: the outer world and an inner sea of blood and tissue fluid that bathes every cell. Only because that inner sea stays constant can the animal move freely through a changing outer world. The American physiologist Walter Cannon later gave the idea its name, homeostasis, from Greek words meaning staying the same.

What gets held steady? Temperature. The amount of water. Blood sugar, which your cells need as fuel and which is dangerous both too high and too low. The acidity of the blood, kept within a very narrow range near a pH of 7.4. The levels of sodium, potassium and calcium. Oxygen and carbon dioxide. Each has a *set point*, a target value, and each has sensors and responses to nudge it back when it drifts. Homeostasis does not mean nothing changes. It means small changes trigger corrections.

A cell does the same thing on its own scale. It holds its internal salt and water in balance with the pumps and channels from the last section. It keeps its pH steady. When a cell's homeostasis fails, the cell dies. When the body's fails, we call it disease. Diabetes is blood sugar homeostasis breaking down. Heatstroke is temperature homeostasis overwhelmed. Much of medicine is the art of helping a body find its set points again.

words.d: the process of keeping conditions inside a cell or body steady while the outside changes
the target value that a body system works to maintain, such as 37 degrees Celsius
a scientist who studies how living bodies work

look.title: The Inner Sea
look.text: Bernard argued that the constancy of the internal environment is the condition for a free and independent life. An animal whose blood and tissue fluid stay steady is no longer at the mercy of every change in the world outside; it can go where it likes because it carries its own environment with it.
look.cite: Claude Bernard, lectures on the properties of living tissues, Paris, 1860s
look.prompt: A lizard's body temperature rises and falls with the air. A mouse's does not. Using Bernard's idea, which animal can be active on a cold night, and what does that freedom cost?

check.q: Which of these is the best example of homeostasis?
choices: A plant growing toward a window
Your body keeping its core temperature near 37 degrees Celsius on a cold day
A cell dividing into two
A muscle getting larger with exercise
check.why: Homeostasis is holding an internal condition steady despite outside change. Core temperature on a cold day is a textbook case.

check.q: What did Claude Bernard mean by the internal environment?
choices: The inside of the nucleus
The organs of the digestive system
The blood and tissue fluid that bathe every cell of the body
The air inside the lungs
check.why: Bernard pointed out that cells never touch the outside world directly. They live in an inner fluid the body keeps constant.

check.q: Which statement about homeostasis is most accurate?
choices: Conditions inside the body never change at all
Only warm-blooded animals have homeostasis
Homeostasis means the body copies the outside conditions
Small drifts away from a set point trigger responses that push conditions back
check.why: Values do drift. Homeostasis is the constant correcting, not the absence of change.

lessons.title: Feedback Loops
lessons.mainIdea: Negative feedback reverses a change to hold a set point; positive feedback amplifies a change to push a process to its finish.
reading: A home thermostat is a machine for homeostasis. It has a sensor that reads the room temperature, a set point you choose, and a response, the furnace. Room gets cold, furnace turns on. Room warms past the set point, furnace turns off. The response undoes the change that triggered it. That is *negative feedback*, and negative here does not mean bad. It means the response pushes in the opposite direction from the change.

Your body runs on negative feedback loops. Sensors in your brain read blood temperature. Too warm, and blood vessels in your skin widen and sweat glands switch on; evaporating sweat carries heat away. Too cold, and skin vessels narrow to keep warm blood deep, and muscles shiver to make heat. After a sugary drink, blood glucose rises. The pancreas releases the hormone insulin, cells take up glucose, and the level falls. Hours later, when glucose dips, the pancreas releases a different hormone, glucagon, and the liver releases stored sugar. Two hormones, pushing opposite ways, hold glucose in a narrow band.

*Positive feedback* does the opposite. The response makes the change bigger. That sounds dangerous, and in a loop that never stops, it would be. But the body uses it for jobs that need to finish fast. When a blood vessel is cut, the first clotting proteins activate more clotting proteins, which activate still more, until a plug seals the wound. During childbirth, each contraction triggers release of a hormone that causes stronger contractions, until the baby is born and the loop ends. Positive feedback drives a process to completion, then stops.

When you meet a new body process, ask which kind of loop it is. Fever is negative feedback with a temporarily raised set point. Thirst is negative feedback for water. A panic that feeds on itself is positive feedback, and so is a runaway rumor. Engineers use the same two ideas in cruise control, in nuclear reactors and in the audio squeal when a microphone hears its own speaker. Cells invented feedback billions of years before we did.

words.d: a loop in which the response reverses the original change, holding a value near its set point
a loop in which the response strengthens the original change until a process is complete
a hormone from the pancreas that signals cells to take up glucose, lowering blood sugar
a chemical messenger carried in the blood from one part of the body to another

look.title: Two Runners, One Hot Day
look.text: Two students run a mile on a 32 degree Celsius afternoon. One drinks water at the halfway point and finishes red-faced and sweaty. The other, who skipped water all day, stops sweating near the end, feels dizzy, and has hot, dry skin. A coach calls for help.
look.prompt: Describe the negative feedback loop that was working in the first runner. Which part of the loop failed in the second runner, and why?

check.q: After a large sugary drink, blood glucose rises and the pancreas releases insulin, which lowers it. What kind of loop is this?
choices: Positive feedback
A concentration gradient
Negative feedback
Osmosis
check.why: The response, insulin, reverses the change, bringing glucose back toward its set point.

check.q: Which is an example of positive feedback?
choices: Shivering when cold
Sweating when hot
Insulin lowering blood sugar
Clotting proteins activating more clotting proteins until a wound seals
check.why: In clotting, each step strengthens the next until the job is done. That is a self-amplifying positive loop.

check.q: If the sensor in a thermostat broke and always reported the room as warm, what would happen?
choices: The furnace would run constantly and overheat the room
The furnace would never turn on and the room would get cold
The furnace would switch on and off rapidly
Nothing would change because the set point is still correct
check.why: A negative feedback loop needs an honest sensor. If the sensor reports warm, the furnace never gets the signal to start.

review.q: Which property of water explains why lakes warm slowly in spring and why your body resists sudden temperature swings?
choices: Hydrogen bonds make water slow to heat and slow to cool
Water is a solvent
Ice is less dense than liquid water
Water is nonpolar
review.why: Breaking and forming many hydrogen bonds absorbs and releases a lot of heat for a small temperature change.

review.q: Which pair correctly matches a macromolecule with its building unit?
choices: Lipid and glucose
Protein and amino acid
Carbohydrate and nucleotide
DNA and fatty acid
review.why: Proteins are chains of amino acids. Carbohydrates are chains of sugars, and DNA is built from nucleotides.

review.q: Why does the acid in the chapter's gelatin experiment reach the center of the small cube but not the large one?
choices: The large cube is made of denser gelatin
Acid diffuses faster in small objects
As a cube grows, its volume increases much faster than its surface area, so the center is farther from any surface
The small cube has more surface area in total
review.why: Doubling the side gives four times the surface but eight times the volume. The center of a big cube is simply far from the edge.

review.q: A cell has a nucleus, mitochondria, a large central vacuole and a cell wall. What is it?
choices: A bacterium
An animal cell
A virus
A plant cell
review.why: A nucleus makes it eukaryotic; the vacuole and wall make it a plant cell. Animal cells have neither wall nor large vacuole.

review.q: Why does Virchow's rule, all cells come from cells, matter for understanding cancer?
choices: It means a tumor is cells dividing when they should not, rather than something forming from nowhere
It means cancer cannot spread
It means cancer cells are not real cells
It means only bacteria cause cancer
review.why: If cells arise only by division, then uncontrolled growth must come from a cell's own division control going wrong.

review.q: A carrier protein moves glucose into a cell from a higher concentration outside to a lower one inside, with no ATP used. What is this called?
choices: Active transport
Facilitated diffusion
Osmosis
Exocytosis
review.why: The movement is down the gradient and costs nothing, but it needs a protein because glucose is polar. That is facilitated diffusion.

review.q: A freshwater fish is moved into seawater. What will osmosis do to its cells at first?
choices: Water will rush in and the cells will swell
Nothing, because fish cells have walls
Water will leave the cells, and they will shrink
Salt will be pumped out automatically at no cost
review.why: Seawater has far more dissolved particles than the fish's cells, so water moves out of the cells toward the salt.

review.q: Which of these is negative feedback?
choices: Contractions triggering stronger contractions during birth
A rumor spreading faster the more people repeat it
Clotting proteins activating more clotting proteins
Shivering when body temperature drops, which produces heat and stops the drop
review.why: The response, shivering, reverses the change. The other three amplify the change.
